name: eccodes
desc: Decode and encode messages in the GRIB 1/2 and BUFR 3/4 formats
why: Decodes GRIB and BUFR weather message formats, a door into how forecast data is actually packed.

brief.what_it_is: ecCodes is a package from ECMWF that provides an API and a set of command-line tools for decoding and encoding weather messages in WMO GRIB edition 1 and 2, BUFR edition 3 and 4, and (decode only) the GTS abbreviated header. The command-line tools give quick access to messages, and C, Fortran 90 and Python interfaces expose the main functionality. It reads and writes binary meteorological message files, and the tools print or change their contents using a key/value model. The executables include grib_ls, grib_dump, grib_get, grib_set, grib_copy, grib_to_netcdf, the matching bufr_ and gts_ tools, and codes_info and codes_count.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents ecCodes as the successor to GRIB-API, offering a simple key/value way to access data from several formats. It is now the primary GRIB encoding and decoding package at ECMWF, and GRIB-API is no longer maintained as of December 2018.
brief.how_it_works: Messages are accessed through key/value functions, so a caller asks for a named key such as a field attribute and gets its value, or sets one. The grib_ functions are kept, and a new codes_ family with the same interface and behaviour works across all supported formats. The command-line tools were built to mirror the old GRIB-API tools' options and behaviour, with bufr_dump as the main difference because it emits JSON.

commands_seen.context: Unpacks the source distribution downloaded from the Releases page.
Creates a separate build directory, as the README asks for an out-of-tree build.
Moves into the build directory before running cmake.

brief.install_notes: Build from the source tarball with cmake and make, then run ctest and make install. Install into a clean directory, since the README says this is strongly recommended. The Python bindings come separately from PyPI with pip3 install eccodes. Other platform guidance is on the Confluence installation page, which I could not load (HTTP 404). Conda-forge also packages it, per the README badges.
brief.standout: The tools share GRIB-API's options and behaviour, so existing scripts can carry over. bufr_dump emits JSON, which is handy for web applications, and it reads the packed binary formats that forecast centres exchange, not just a viewer for them.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub README badges the project as Graduated under ECMWF's software maturity guidelines. The Confluence news lists ecCodes 2.50.0 released Oct 14, 2026, after 2.49.0 (Sept 23, 2026) and 2.48.0 (Jul 15, 2026), so releases are regular.
brief.caveats: The GTS format is decode-only. The GRIB-API Fortran 77 interface is no longer available. Building from source needs cmake and a C toolchain, and the README points to the Confluence pages for the full installation guide. Licensed under Apache 2.0. The GRIB-API migration is advised for existing users.
quotes: ecCodes is now the primary GRIB encoding/decoding package used at ECMWF.
A significant difference compared with GRIB-API tools is that bufr_dump produces output in JSON format suitable for many web based applications.
It is designed to provide the user with a simple set of functions to access data from several formats with a key/value approach.

judge.reason: A specialist gateway into how forecast data is packed and exchanged, ecCodes makes the otherwise opaque GRIB and BUFR formats inspectable and editable.

entry.title: eccodes
entry.tldr: ECMWF's toolkit for reading and writing GRIB and BUFR, the packed binary formats weather centres use to exchange forecasts and observations.
entry.deeper_look:
ecCodes is a package from ECMWF, the European weather forecasting centre. It provides command-line tools and C, Fortran 90 and Python interfaces for decoding and encoding WMO GRIB (editions 1 and 2) and BUFR (editions 3 and 4) messages. It can also decode, but not encode, the GTS abbreviated header.

The core idea is a key/value model. Each message is a set of named keys, and you ask for a key to read it or assign one to change it. The tools are thin layers over that idea: `grib_ls` lists messages, `grib_dump` shows every key, `grib_get` pulls out chosen values, `grib_set` rewrites them, and `grib_copy` filters messages into new files. The `bufr_` and `gts_` tools follow the same pattern.

The interesting part is what it exposes. Forecast fields and observation reports are not stored as friendly tables. They are tightly packed binary with compression and layered code tables, and ecCodes is how most people get at what is inside. Poking at a file with `grib_dump` is a quick way to see how a forecast is actually packed and described.

It is the successor to GRIB-API and the primary GRIB encoding and decoding package at ECMWF. The tools were built to mirror the old options and behaviour. The main difference is that `bufr_dump` emits JSON.
entry.install:
brew install eccodes
# you need your own GRIB or BUFR file to try the tools on; the brief does not name a sample dataset
# Python bindings come separately: pip3 install eccodes

Shows how to dump a BUFR message, whose output is JSON.

entry.whats_unique: It is the reference toolkit from the forecasting centre that works with these formats every day, and one key/value interface covers GRIB, BUFR and GTS headers. The tools stay compatible with GRIB-API's options.
entry.caveats: You need GRIB or BUFR files of your own to work on, and GTS support is decode-only.
